title: Treesa Jolly and Gayatri Gopichand Assure India's First Women's Doubles World Championships Medal in 15 Years
excerpt: The Indian pair reached the semifinals at the home BWF World Championships in New Delhi, ending a drought that stretched back to Jwala Gutta and Ashwini Ponnappa's 2011 bronze.
body:
• Treesa Jolly and Gayatri Gopichand have reached the semifinals of the BWF World Championships 2026 in New Delhi, assuring India at least a bronze medal in women's doubles.
  • The achievement ends a 15-year wait for an Indian women's doubles medal at the World Championships, the last being Jwala Gutta and Ashwini Ponnappa's bronze in 2011.
  • The duo defeated Japan's seventh seeds Rin Iwanaga and Kie Nakanishi 21-16, 21-12 in the Round of 16 before overcoming China's fourth seeds Jia Yi Fan and Zhang Shi Xian in the quarterfinals.
  • Two-time bronze medallists Satwiksairaj Rankireddy and Chirag Shetty also advanced to the quarterfinals in men's doubles.

Treesa Jolly and Gayatri Gopichand have written themselves into Indian badminton history. The women's doubles pair reached the semifinals of the BWF World Championships 2026 in New Delhi on Thursday, guaranteeing India at least a bronze medal and ending a 15-year drought in the event.

The last Indian women's doubles pair to medal at the World Championships was Jwala Gutta and Ashwini Ponnappa, who claimed bronze at the 2011 edition in London. Since then, Indian women's doubles has endured a barren stretch at the sport's most prestigious individual tournament.

A Clinical Run Through the Draw

Treesa and Gayatri's path to the medal round has been marked by composure and aggressive play. In their Round of 16 clash, they dismantled Japan's seventh seeds Rin Iwanaga and Kie Nakanishi 21-16, 21-12 in straight games, a result that made them the first Indian women's doubles pair in 11 years to reach the World Championships quarterfinals.

"We came here with a goal, and we are focusing on that."

— Treesa Jolly, after the Round of 16 victory

The quarterfinal against China's fourth seeds Jia Yi Fan and Zhang Shi Xian presented a far sterner test, but the Indian pair's combination of Treesa's powerful backcourt smashes and Gayatri's deft net play proved decisive. The Indira Gandhi Arena crowd — louder and larger than any preceding session — carried the duo through the pressure points.

Home Crowd Fuels Historic Campaign

India is hosting the BWF World Championships for the first time, and the home support has been a tangible factor. Crowds at the Indira Gandhi Arena in New Delhi have swelled with each passing day, with Thursday's sessions drawing the biggest turnouts of the tournament.

The pair's coach Pullela Gopichand — Gayatri's father and one of Indian badminton's most influential figures — has overseen their development since their junior days. Their partnership, which began as teenagers, has matured through titles at the Badminton Asia Mixed Team Championship, the All England semifinals, and qualification for the BWF World Tour Finals in Hangzhou last year.

Mixed Day for India's Other Medal Hopes

It was a day of contrasts for India's contingent. Two-time bronze medallists Satwiksairaj Rankireddy and Chirag Shetty advanced to the men's doubles quarterfinals after a hard-fought three-game battle against Malaysia's Junaidi Arif and Yap Roy King, winning 21-23, 21-19, 21-17. They will face China's third seeds Liang Wei Keng and Wang Chang.

However, PV Sindhu's bid for a record sixth World Championships medal ended in the Round of 16. The two-time champion fell to China's third seed Wang Zhi Yi 21-11, 15-21, 21-17 in a match where she could not sustain the momentum from a strong second game. Ayush Shetty's campaign also ended with a straight-games loss to Indonesia's Alwi Farhan.

What's Next

Treesa and Gayatri's semifinal opponent and match schedule will be confirmed following the remaining quarterfinals. With a medal already secured, the pressure shifts — they can play freely for a shot at gold or silver.

For Indian badminton, the result is validation of a long investment in women's doubles. The country has historically excelled in singles — through Saina Nehwal, Sindhu, and Lakshya Sen — but doubles success at the highest level has been elusive. Treesa and Gayatri's semifinal berth suggests that gap is closing, according to the Times of India and HiSporty.
